title: Hindsight-Privileged RLVR: Single-Rollout Token Credit Without Group Sampling

paper.title: Hindsight-Privileged RLVR: Single-Rollout Token Credit Without Group Sampling
paper.abstract: Abstract Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) trains language models from checked task outcomes, but assigning a terminal reward to individual reasoning tokens or actions remains difficult. Group-relative methods such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) sample several attempts per prompt, but lose their reward-based learning signal when all attempts receive the same outcome. We propose Hindsight-Privileged RLVR (HP-RLVR), a single-rollout method that turns a completed trajectory’s own future into token-level update weights. The generating policy snapshot scores each eligible token under its causal history and under a hindsight context containing the realized future and verifier feedback. A normalized Jensen–Shannon divergence between the two views weights the reward relative to a historical baseline, yielding bounded token credit for both successful and failed attempts, with no reference solution or learned critic. In paired Qwen3-8B runs over a shared 100 100 -step schedule, HP-RLVR trains 1.21 × 1.21\times , 1.46 × 1.46\times , and 2.30 × 2.30\times faster than GRPO on mathematics, code generation, and ALFWorld, using one eighth the rollouts per prompt. Accuracy is comparable overall, with HP-RLVR ahead on mathematics at all three sizes and GRPO ahead on code and ALFWorld. In ALFWorld, 43.2 % 43.2\% (4B) and 49.0 % 49.0\% (8B) of GRPO’s gradient-norm records are zero, versus none for HP-RLVR.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Figure 1: Qwen3-8B training cost at four prompts per step and 100 100 steps. HP-RLVR uses group size G = 1 G{=}1 , versus GRPO’s G = 8 G{=}8 . Bars are relative to GRPO, with labels above each pair showing speedup. Figure 2: Overview of HP-RLVR’s single-rollout training pipeline with training-only hindsight. After generation, the frozen generating policy scores the trajectory under causal and hindsight contexts, without additional sampling. The paired profiles show full-vocabulary distributions at the same token position. Normalized JSD weights the historically centered verifier reward to produce token credit. Bars are schematic, and dashed frames group stages. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) trains language models through outcomes checked by symbolic verifiers, test suites, or interactive environments ( Guo et al., 2025 ) . Terminal verification supplies supervision without labeling every intermediate decision. Turning that supervision into efficient learning, however, requires addressing both the cost of obtaining an update signal and its allocation within a trajectory. First, group-relative learning obtains its signal through repeated attempts. Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) compares multiple responses to each prompt, replacing a learned critic with a baseline computed from group rewards ( Shao et al., 2024 ) . This comparison requires multiple rollouts, yet homogeneous outcomes give zero reward advantages ( Yu et al., 2025 ) . Additional sampling therefore incurs cost without necessarily supplying an informative comparison. Second, comparisons between complete attempts leave credit coarse within each attempt. Outcome-supervised GRPO broadcasts a trajectory’s advantage to its tokens ( Shao et al., 2024 ) , despite the different roles of intermediate decisions in reasoning and multi-turn interaction ( Lightman et al., 2023 ; Feng et al., 2025 ) . Process supervision supplies intermediate labels ( Lightman et al., 2023 ) , implicit process rewards learn dense signals ( Yuan et al., 2024 ; Cui et al., 2025 ) , and intermediate-value estimation can require additional continuations ( Kazemnejad et al., 2025 ) . These approaches motivate a complementary question: can a single verified attempt, whether successful or failed, itself supply a finer learning signal? A completed attempt’s realized future provides context for revisiting earlier decisions ( Harutyunyan et al., 2019 ; Mesnard et al., 2021 ) . We introduce Hindsight-Privileged RLVR (HP-RLVR), which uses this future as training-only privilege ( Fig. 2 ). The generating policy compares token distributions with and without the future and verifier feedback. Historical reward centering directs the update and can give failures negative credit, while normalized Jensen–Shannon divergence supplies bounded, nonnegative token weights. This yields local credit from one rollout per prompt, without a reference solution or learned critic ( Sec. 3 ). We evaluate Qwen3 models (1.7B/4B/8B) ( Yang et al., 2025 ) on mathematics, code generation, and ALFWorld ( Shridhar et al., 2020 ) . Figure 1 summarizes the Qwen3-8B cost benefit at a shared prompt and step budget, using one eighth as many rollouts per prompt. Task accuracy and training-signal diagnostics assess the resulting single-rollout updates ( Figs. 3 and 4 ). Our contributions are: • A single-rollout hindsight construction using the generating policy and its own realized future, without reference solutions or a learned critic ( Sec. 3.2 ). • A bounded token-credit rule for both successful and failed trajectories, combining historical reward centering with normalized distributional divergence ( Sec. 3.3 ). • Lower training cost at a shared step schedule, with accuracy comparisons and protocol diagnostics ( Sec. 4 ).

sections.heading: Outcome-based and hindsight credit assignment.
sections.text: Methods for assigning local credit differ in how they obtain information beyond a terminal reward. Learned value baselines estimate future returns ( Schulman et al., 2016 ) , and RUDDER redistributes delayed rewards through a return predictor ( Arjona-Medina et al., 2019 ) . In language-model reasoning, process supervision supplies intermediate labels ( Lightman et al., 2023 ) , implicit process rewards learn dense signals from outcome supervision ( Yuan et al., 2024 ; Cui et al., 2025 ) , and VinePPO estimates intermediate values through additional continuations ( Kazemnejad et al., 2025 ) . Hindsight credit assignment instead uses observed future information to revisit past actions ( Harutyunyan et al., 2019 ) . Counterfactual credit assignment conditions value functions on suitable future events to reduce policy-gradient variance ( Mesnard et al., 2021 ) . This distinction also matters for multi-turn agents. GiGPO augments episode-level group advantages with step-level comparisons at repeated states across sampled trajectories ( Feng et al., 2025 ) . HCAPO uses the language model as a post-hoc critic and combines hindsight action evaluation with multi-scale advantages ( Tan et al., 2026 ) . HP-RLVR draws on the same idea of revisiting decisions after completion, but constructs its weights from the full-vocabulary divergence between two views of the generating snapshot.

sections.heading: Privileged supervision and failures.
sections.text: On-policy distillation scores student-generated sequences with a teacher ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ) . OPSD conditions the same model on privileged reference information ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) . Feedback-based self-distillation obtains privilege from interaction ( Hübotter et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026 ; Yeo et al., 2026 ) . H 2 SD uses verified student responses to refine successful trajectories and reference hints to correct failures ( Cai et al., 2026 ) . HP-RLVR instead uses an unsigned divergence to weight reward-based updates, including updates on failures without a corrective reference. Negative reinforcement can itself improve reasoning ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) , but update dynamics depend on weighting ( Chen et al., 2026 ) , loss normalization, and length dynamics ( Liu et al., 2025 ; Yu et al., 2025 ) . HP-RLVR and GRPO use trajectory-balanced loss reduction, and we report training-signal availability under this shared protocol ( Sec. 4.4 ).

sections.heading: 4 Experiments
sections.text: Our evaluation tests whether training-only hindsight can replace group sampling at lower computational cost, and how that substitution affects task accuracy and the availability of a training signal. We study sequence-level verification in mathematics and code generation, and sparse terminal rewards in multi-turn ALFWorld interaction.

sections.heading: 4.1 Experimental setup
sections.text: We evaluate Qwen3-1.7B, 4B, and 8B ( Yang et al., 2025 ) , comparing HP-RLVR ( G = 1 G{=}1 ) with a critic-free GRPO control ( G = 8 G{=}8 ). Paired runs share task data, seed 42 42 , LoRA configuration ( Hu et al., 2021 ) , Adam settings ( Kingma and Ba, 2014 ) , and one PPO epoch per rollout step. Both use full-support training sampling and trajectory-balanced loss reduction. We evaluate at steps 25 25 , 50 50 , 75 75 , and 100 100 . A training step comprises one rollout-and-training iteration, with run-specific trajectory budgets and internal optimizer-step counts. Run-specific batching records appear in appendix D.1 . Both methods use LoRA rank 64 64 , α = 128 \alpha=128 , and dropout 0 0 , applied to attention and MLP projections, with Adam betas 0.9 0.9 and 0.999 0.999 , zero weight decay, a constant learning rate of 5 × 10 − 6 5\times 10^{-6} , gradient clipping 1.0 1.0 , and a PPO clip range of 0.2 0.2 . Each step takes one optimization epoch over its rollout batch, and the shared schedule runs 100 100 rollout-and-training steps with checkpoints every 25 25 steps. Training steps count rollout-and-training iterations, separately from internal optimizer steps and log records. Mathematics trains on a 30 30 k-prompt OpenThoughts mixture ( Guha et al., 2025 ) , and code generation trains on 800 800 problems divided into 60 % 60\% standard-I/O and 40 % 40\% function-call tasks. Both cap training responses at 1,024 1{,}024 tokens. ALFWorld uses four prompts per rollout step, 50 50 turns, an eight-turn retained history, a 4,096 4{,}096 -token per-turn response cap, and an 8,192 8{,}192 -token training context. Mathematics uses an official symbolic verifier, code generation a test harness, and ALFWorld the environment’s terminal success signal. Both methods sample at temperature 1 1 without top- p p or top- k k truncation, which keeps the sampled distribution, the behavior scoring, and the likelihood-ratio denominator aligned. At each generated position j j the rollout engine records the token y j y_{j} and its generation-time log-probability, which supplies the behavior denominator of Eq. 8 ; for agents, h j h_{j} contains the retained observation–action history rather than necessarily the entire episode. The full behavior distribution of Eq. 6 is obtained by replaying the same history with the generating snapshot, and a check at the first update replays current log-probabilities against that record, aborting the run on a mismatch rather than biasing the ratios. The exact divergence of Eq. 7 is evaluated over the full vocabulary in groups of token positions, with no top- k k or restricted-support approximation: stored token weights require O ⁡ ( T ) O(T) memory and temporary divergence calculations O ⁡ ( C ​ V ) O(CV) for T T positions, vocabulary size V V , and groups of at most C C positions, excluding model states and activations. Mathematics uses AIME24, AIME25, and HMMT25 ( Balunović et al., 2025 ; HMMT, 2025 ) , with 30 30 problems per benchmark and 12 12 samples per problem, thinking enabled, temperature 1 1 , top- p p 0.95 0.95 , and a 38,912 38{,}912 -token response cap. Avg@ 12 12 averages sampled correctness and Pass@ 12 12 measures whether any sample solves a problem. Mathematics aggregates average the three benchmarks. Code evaluates at temperature 0.2 0.2 on all 1,055 1{,}055 LiveCodeBench release- 6 6 problems ( Jain et al., 2024 ) , with Pass@ 1 1 and Pass@ 8 8 computed as eight-sample estimates from a common dump. ALFWorld reports the mean success rate across in-distribution (ID, 140 140 games) and out-of-distribution (OOD, 134 134 games) splits ( Shridhar et al., 2020 ) , evaluating one episode per game under the 50 50 -turn protocol. Each method has one training seed. All timings use 8 Ascend 910B NPUs.

sections.heading: 4.3 Task accuracy under single-rollout training
sections.text: To assess the performance–time tradeoff, Fig. 3 pairs each configuration’s best observed task score within 100 100 steps with its measured complete-run training time. sections.text: The mathematics comparison combines a short training cap with long evaluation responses. sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: HP-RLVR assigns token credit from one rollout per prompt: historical reward centering sets the update direction, while bounded, nonnegative JSD weights from causal and hindsight scoring allocate its magnitude. This rule applies to successful and failed trajectories and can give failures negative credit without a corrective reference. At a shared prompt and 100 100 -step budget, paired Qwen3-8B runs train 1.21 × 1.21\times , 1.46 × 1.46\times , and 2.30 × 2.30\times faster than G = 8 G{=}8 GRPO on mathematics, code, and ALFWorld, using one eighth as many rollouts per prompt. Accuracy is comparable overall, with HP-RLVR ahead on mathematics at all three sizes and GRPO ahead on code and ALFWorld. In ALFWorld, 43.2 % 43.2\% (4B) and 49.0 % 49.0\% (8B) of GRPO’s gradient-norm records are zero, versus none for HP-RLVR.

Group-relative methods such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) sample several attempts per prompt, but lose their reward-based learning signal when all attempts receive the same outcome. We propose Hindsight-Privileged RLVR (HP-RLVR), a single-rollout method that turns a completed trajectory’s own future into token-level update weights. The generating policy snapshot scores each eligible token under its causal history and under a hindsight context containing the realized future and verifier feedback. A normalized Jensen–Shannon divergence between the two views weights the reward relative to a historical baseline, yielding bounded token credit for both successful and failed attempts, with no reference solution or learned critic. In paired Qwen3-8B runs over a shared 100 100 -step schedule, HP-RLVR trains 1.21 × 1.21\times , 1.46 × 1.46\times , and 2.30 × 2.30\times faster than GRPO on mathematics, code generation, and ALFWorld, using one eighth the rollouts per prompt. Accuracy is comparable overall, with HP-RLVR ahead on mathematics at all three sizes and GRPO ahead on code and ALFWorld. In ALFWorld, 43.2 % 43.2\% (4B) and 49.0 % 49.0\% (8B) of GRPO’s gradient-norm records are zero, versus none for HP-RLVR. 1 Introduction Figure 1: Qwen3-8B training cost at four prompts per step and 100 100 steps. HP-RLVR uses group size G = 1 G{=}1 , versus GRPO’s G = 8 G{=}8 . Bars are relative to GRPO, with labels above each pair showing speedup. Figure 2: Overview of HP-RLVR’s single-rollout training pipeline with training-only hindsight. After generation, the frozen generating policy scores the trajectory under causal and hindsight contexts, without additional sampling. The paired profiles show full-vocabulary distributions at the same token position. Normalized JSD weights the historically centered verifier reward to produce token credit. Bars are schematic, and dashed frames group stages. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) trains language models through outcomes checked by symbolic verifiers, test suites, or interactive environments ( Guo et al., 2025 ) . Terminal verification supplies supervision without labeling every intermediate decision. Turning that supervision into efficient learning, however, requires addressing both the cost of obtaining an update signal and its allocation within a trajectory. First, group-relative learning obtains its signal through repeated attempts. Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) compares multiple responses to each prompt, replacing a learned critic with a baseline computed from group rewards ( Shao et al., 2024 ) . This comparison requires multiple rollouts, yet homogeneous outcomes give zero reward advantages ( Yu et al., 2025 ) . Additional sampling therefore incurs cost without necessarily supplying an informative comparison. Second, comparisons between complete attempts leave credit coarse within each attempt. Outcome-supervised GRPO broadcasts a trajectory’s advantage to its tokens ( Shao et al., 2024 ) , despite the different roles of intermediate decisions in reasoning and multi-turn interaction ( Lightman et al., 2023 ; Feng et al., 2025 ) . Process supervision supplies intermediate labels ( Lightman et al., 2023 ) , implicit process rewards learn dense signals ( Yuan et al., 2024 ; Cui et al., 2025 ) , and intermediate-value estimation can require additional continuations ( Kazemnejad et al., 2025 ) . These approaches motivate a complementary question: can a single verified attempt, whether successful or failed, itself supply a finer learning signal? A completed attempt’s realized future provides context for revisiting earlier decisions ( Harutyunyan et al., 2019 ; Mesnard et al., 2021 ) . We introduce Hindsight-Privileged RLVR (HP-RLVR), which uses this future as training-only privilege ( Fig. 2 ). The generating policy compares token distributions with and without the future and verifier feedback. Historical reward centering directs the update and can give failures negative credit, while normalized Jensen–Shannon divergence supplies bounded, nonnegative token weights. This yields local credit from one rollout per prompt, without a reference solution or learned critic ( Sec. 3 ). We evaluate Qwen3 models (1.7B/4B/8B) ( Yang et al., 2025 ) on mathematics, code generation, and ALFWorld ( Shridhar et al., 2020 ) . Figure 1 summarizes the Qwen3-8B cost benefit at a shared prompt and step budget, using one eighth as many rollouts per prompt. Task accuracy and training-signal diagnostics assess the resulting single-rollout updates ( Figs. 3 and 4 ). Our contributions are: • A single-rollout hindsight construction using the generating policy and its own realized future, without reference solutions or a learned critic ( Sec. 3.2 ). • A bounded token-credit rule for both successful and failed trajectories, combining historical reward centering with normalized distributional divergence ( Sec. 3.3 ). • Lower training cost at a shared step schedule, with accuracy comparisons and protocol diagnostics ( Sec. 4 ). 2 Background and Related Work 2.1 Related work Outcome-based and hindsight credit assignment. Methods for assigning local credit differ in how they obtain information beyond a terminal reward. Learned value baselines estimate future returns ( Schulman et al., 2016 ) , and RUDDER redistributes delayed rewards through a return predictor ( Arjona-Medina et al., 2019 ) . In language-model reasoning, process supervision supplies intermediate labels ( Lightman et al., 2023 ) , implicit process rewards learn dense signals from outcome supervision ( Yuan et al., 2024 ; Cui et al., 2025 ) , and VinePPO estimates intermediate values through additional continuations ( Kazemnejad et al., 2025 ) . Hindsight credit assignment instead uses observed future information to revisit past actions ( Harutyunyan et al., 2019 ) . Counterfactual credit assignment conditions value functions on suitable future events to reduce policy-gradient variance ( Mesnard et al., 2021 ) . This distinction also matters for multi-turn agents. GiGPO augments episode-level group advantages with step-level comparisons at repeated states across sampled trajectories ( Feng et al., 2025 ) . HCAPO uses the language model as a post-hoc critic and combines hindsight action evaluation with multi-scale advantages ( Tan et al., 2026 ) . HP-RLVR draws on the same idea of revisiting decisions after completion, but constructs its weights from the full-vocabulary divergence between two views of the generating snapshot. Privileged supervision and failures. On-policy distillation scores student-generated sequences with a teacher ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ) . OPSD conditions the same model on privileged reference information ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) . Feedback-based self-distillation obtains privilege from interaction ( Hübotter et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026 ; Yeo et al., 2026 ) . H 2 SD uses verified student responses to refine successful trajectories and reference hints to correct failures ( Cai et al., 2026 ) . HP-RLVR instead uses an unsigned divergence to weight reward-based updates, including updates on failures without a corrective reference. Negative reinforcement can itself improve reasoning ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) , but update dynamics depend on weighting ( Chen et al., 2026 ) , loss normalization, and length dynamics ( Liu et al., 2025 ; Yu et al., 2025 ) .
